results.title: Moving From Manual Reverse Engineering of UEFI Modules To Dynamic Emulation of UEFI Firmware - SentinelLabs
results.snippet: The main reason for that is that UEFI modules typically execute early in the boot process, long before an OS kernel is loaded into memory. To accommodate these shortcomings, *efi\_dxe\_emulator* implements some of the most heavily-used UEFI services on its own. In addition to the core UEFI services, the emulator also implements a PE loader (so as to load UEFI images into memory), a simple heap, a handle database and a basic interactive debugger which lets you step through the emulated code. The run function in *os/uefi/uefi.py* is the main function of UEFI execution, however it is executed after the run function of *loader/pe\_uefi.py* did the heavy lifting of loading the modules and installing the hooks and protocols. Figure 14 - Executing a UEFI module with variables values loaded from a file. To some degree, emulating a single UEFI module is equivalent to loading a binary without mapping all the shared libraries it depends on to function properly.

Unified Extensible Firmware Interface - ArchWiki
results.snippet: The Unified Extensible Firmware Interface **(UEFI)** is an interface between operating systems and firmware. It provides a standard environment for booting an operating system and running pre-boot applications. See Arch boot process for their differences and the boot process using UEFI. To set up UEFI boot loaders, see Arch boot process#Boot loader. Under UEFI, every program whether it is an operating system loader or a utility (e.g. a memory testing or recovery tool), should be an EFI application corresponding to the UEFI firmware bitness/architecture. An x64 UEFI firmware does not include support for launching 32-bit EFI applications (unlike x86\_64 Linux and Windows versions which include such support). The firmware bitness can be checked from a booted operating system. So, if you have a 32-bit version of Windows booted in UEFI mode, you have a 32-bit UEFI. For 64-bit Windows on a 64-bit UEFI, it will be `System Type: x64-based PC` and `BIOS mode: UEFI`.

results.title: Reverse Engineering UEFI Firmware – Technology & Policy – Jethro Beekman
results.snippet: *Wait what, run UEFI PE modules?* Yes, I wrote a tool called `efiperun` that can load PE modules into memory and simulate enough of what an UEFI environment is supposed to look like to actually run them. With `efiperun` you can actually write code that calls into loaded EFI modules, which makes it easy to test installed interfaces. The password control program has an interesting function at offset `0x8cc` that calls only `SetMem`, `CopyMem` and the Crypto and Translate services. The password control program calls a function in the Crypto service at offset `0x26e0`, which references three GUIDs that I hadn’t seen before:. All in all this suggests that the Crypto service is a front for the cryptographic routines in `SystemCryptSvcRt.efi` and that the password control program calls SHA256. I assume the input to the function at offset `0xce0` is the password hash from the password control program, but what is the data in “LenovoHddSecInfoVar”?
